name: Developer
desc: 60 random questions from a 100-question CCDVF bank: building with the Messages API, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP - agents and workflows, API mechanics, prompting, evaluation, tools and security - weighted to the exam's eight-domain blueprint.

questions.q: A lender's loan-pack service always runs the same four steps in the same order: extract fields from the application, check them against policy rules, draft a summary, and queue it for an underwriter. Auditors must be able to replay every step, and the steps never change with the input. Which architecture fits?
options: An autonomous agent given all four capabilities as tools and left to decide which to use, so the system adapts to each application it receives
A supervisor agent that spawns one subagent per step and lets them agree among themselves on the order in which the steps should run each time
A workflow in which code fixes the order of the four steps and calls Claude inside each one, so every run follows the same replayable path
One long prompt that lists the four steps and asks Claude to work through them and return the finished pack in a single response each time
questions.explain: The path is fixed and auditors need replay, so code should own the order and Claude should do the work inside each step. An agent earns its extra cost only when the path emerges at run time. A supervisor negotiating step order makes runs differ, and one long prompt hides the intermediate steps that auditors want to inspect.
questions.constraint: fixed order of steps, replayable by auditors
breaks: autonomy adds nothing for a fixed path and makes the order vary between runs
the order is negotiated at run time, so a run cannot be replayed step by step
all steps collapse into one call, so auditors cannot replay or inspect any individual step
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A support team wants Claude to investigate failed deliveries. The useful steps differ for every case: some need the carrier's tracking history, some need a warehouse check, some need neither. The team cannot list the branches in advance. Which design fits best?
options: An agent loop with the relevant lookup tools, where Claude chooses the next step from each result, and a cap on iterations
A fixed workflow with twelve hard-coded branches, one for each failure pattern the team has seen so far, and a catch-all branch for everything else
A single Claude call that receives every tool's output for every case up front, so that no decision about which lookup to run is ever needed
A prompt chain of five fixed stages that always runs carrier, warehouse and refund checks in turn and passes each result forward to the next
questions.explain: When the path depends on what each result shows, the model should pick the next step and a loop cap should bound cost. A fixed branch list needs the very knowledge the team lacks, running every lookup wastes cost, and a fixed chain cannot adapt to a case.
questions.constraint: path depends on intermediate results and cannot be listed in advance
breaks: the branches cannot be enumerated in advance, so the catch-all grows into the real design
runs every lookup for every case, wasting cost and context on irrelevant data
a fixed chain cannot skip or add steps when a case does not need them
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A small team wants an agent that works through long coding tasks asynchronously: it must read files, run commands and edit code in a sandbox. They do not want to write the agent loop, tool execution or sandbox infrastructure themselves. Which option fits?
options: The Messages API with a hand-written loop, because direct model access is the option meant for long-running asynchronous work on a sandbox
A single request per task with extended output length, since a long enough response can replace the loop, the tools and the sandbox altogether
A self-hosted sandbox on the team's own servers that runs the commands, because the harness itself must also be built and operated by the team
Claude Managed Agents with a cloud environment, so Anthropic provides the harness and runs the sandbox, and the team defines only the tasks
questions.explain: Managed Agents provides a pre-built harness plus managed infrastructure and suits long-running, asynchronous work; a cloud environment means Anthropic runs the sandbox. The Messages API is the choice for custom loops and fine-grained control, which this team explicitly does not want.
questions.constraint: no appetite to build the loop, tool execution or sandbox
breaks: the Messages API is for custom loops, which is the work the team wants to avoid
one response cannot read files, run commands or edit code in a sandbox
self-hosting means the team runs the sandbox, which is the burden they want to avoid
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A healthcare company's compliance rules forbid sending data to any service that is not eligible for zero data retention. It still wants Claude Managed Agents rather than building its own harness. Which statement fits the requirement?
options: Use the default cloud environment, since a sandbox that Anthropic runs inherits the ZDR terms of the organisation's main API agreement automatically
Use a self-hosted sandbox, because Managed Agents is not eligible for ZDR except in its self-hosted form
Add a system prompt asking the agent to forget session data once each task completes, which satisfies a zero data retention requirement in practice
Switch to the Message Batches API for the same workload, because batch processing is the only mode in which responses are never stored by the platform
questions.explain: The Managed Agents page states it is not eligible for ZDR except for self-hosted Managed Agents, so the compliance rule decides the environment: self-hosted sandbox. The cloud environment is the near-miss; it is easier to start with but sits outside ZDR. A prompt instruction does not change what is retained.
questions.constraint: ZDR eligibility is mandatory
breaks: the cloud environment is not covered: ZDR applies only to the self-hosted form
a prompt request is not a retention control
batch mode is not a ZDR exemption and does not provide a managed agent harness
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A pipeline first classifies each incoming ticket as billing, technical or account, then handles it with a prompt written for that category. Classification is cheap and the handling prompts differ a lot. Which pattern is this, and why is it a sound choice?
options: An evaluator-optimizer loop, because a first pass labels the ticket and a second pass improves the label until it meets the required quality
A routing workflow, which sends each input to a specialised prompt so each prompt stays short and focused on one category, one per category
An orchestrator-worker system, because a central model breaks the ticket into subtasks that it hands out to workers it creates on demand
Parallelisation by voting, because the same ticket is sent to three prompts at once and the answers are compared to choose a consensus result
questions.explain: Classify-then-dispatch is a routing workflow: the branch is chosen by a label and each handler prompt can be tuned for its category. It is not an orchestrator that invents subtasks, and no output is being scored and revised.
questions.constraint: classification is cheap and the handling prompts differ by category
breaks: nothing here scores and revises an output; it only branches on a label
the branch is a fixed label lookup, not run-time task decomposition
only one specialised prompt runs per ticket; there is no comparison across prompts
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: An Agent SDK job sets max_turns to 4. In a test run the agent makes four tool-calling turns and has all the information it needs, yet the run ends with an error_max_turns result and no final answer. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The agent stopped early because its context filled up, so the fix is to raise the model's output length rather than the turn limit for the run
Tool turns are counted twice, once for the request and once for the result, so max_turns should be set to twice the number of tool calls expected
error_max_turns only appears when the budget is exceeded, so max_budget_usd should be raised and the turn limit can stay unchanged for the job
The final text-only response counts as a turn too, so with four tool turns the limit must be at least five
questions.explain: Each turn that calls tools counts, plus one for the final text-only response; without that extra turn the run ends with error_max_turns and no final response. The budget cap is a separate limit with its own subtype, so raising it would not help.
questions.constraint: four tool turns plus a final answer need a limit of five
breaks: the limit that was hit is the turn limit, not the output length
turns are not counted per request and result; only the extra final response adds one
the budget limit has its own subtype, error_max_budget_usd
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A nightly job built on the Agent SDK reports success whenever the loop finishes without an exception. One night it silently stopped at the spend cap and returned half the work. Which change makes the job report correctly?
options: Read the ResultMessage subtype and treat only the success subtype as done, handling error_max_turns and error_max_budget_usd as incomplete
Check that the final text block is non-empty, since a limit always produces an empty final message and a finished run always produces some text
Wrap the loop in a try/except block and mark failure on any exception, because hitting a limit raises an error that the caller can catch
Remove the spend cap so the loop can always run to completion, and rely on the cloud provider's billing alerts to catch runaway usage instead
questions.explain: The result message carries a subtype that says whether the task succeeded or hit a limit, and limits arrive as result subtypes rather than exceptions. A non-empty final text proves nothing, and deleting the cap removes the safety net instead of reporting the outcome.
questions.constraint: limits surface as ResultMessage subtypes
breaks: a limit can leave partial text, so non-empty text does not prove completion
limits are reported as result subtypes, not as exceptions
removing the cap trades one failure for an uncapped bill and still hides incomplete runs
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: An SDK application registers two PreToolUse hooks for the Bash tool. One returns allow for commands on the team's safe-list. The other returns deny for anything containing rm -rf. A command matches both rules. A developer assumes whichever hook was registered first will decide. What actually happens?
options: The call is allowed, because the earlier-registered hook decides and its allow stops any later hook from changing the outcome for the command
The user is prompted to approve, because conflicting decisions between hooks always fall back to an ask step so that a person settles the tie
The call is denied, because when PreToolUse hooks disagree deny takes priority over every other decision
The result is undefined, because hooks run in parallel and whichever finishes last overwrites the earlier decision for that call every time
questions.explain: When multiple PreToolUse hooks return different decisions, deny outranks defer, which outranks ask, which outranks allow. Hook completion order is non-deterministic, so each hook should act independently. An allow hook cannot rescue a command another hook denies.
questions.constraint: two hooks disagree on one call
breaks: registration order does not decide; decisions are merged by priority
ask ranks below deny, so it only wins against allow
completion order is non-deterministic, which is why priority rules, not timing, decide
questions.chapter: Hooks

questions.q: A settings file in an SDK application has a deny rule for writes under /etc. A custom PreToolUse hook approves a write to /etc/hosts because the path is on its allowlist. What is the outcome?
options: The write is allowed, because a hook runs before the rules and its allow decision is final for the tool call it was returned for
The write is allowed only in bypassPermissions mode, because that mode lets hooks decide while the rules are applied in other modes only
The write triggers the canUseTool callback, because a conflict between a hook and a rule always escalates to the application for approval
The write is denied, because a hook's allow does not skip the deny-rule step, which is evaluated regardless of the hook result
questions.explain: A hook that returns allow does not skip the deny-rule and ask-rule steps, so the settings deny rule still blocks the write. Hooks are a way to add decisions, not to override the declarative rules.
questions.constraint: a deny rule and an allowing hook both match
breaks: an allow from a hook does not override deny rules
deny rules still apply in every permission mode
a matching deny rule ends the evaluation; the callback is not consulted
questions.chapter: Hooks

questions.q: A team registers a PostToolUse hook that returns a deny decision for any Write to the .env file. In testing, the .env file is still overwritten. What should they change?
options: Raise the hook's timeout so the PostToolUse check has time to finish and stop the write, since a slow hook is the usual cause of missed blocks
Move the check to a PreToolUse hook, because PostToolUse fires after the tool already ran and can only report back
Add a stronger line to the system prompt telling the agent never to write .env, and keep the hook as a second layer for logging
Return exit code 2 from the PostToolUse hook, because that code makes the harness undo the completed file write and restore the old contents
questions.explain: PostToolUse runs after the tool, so it can surface a message but cannot prevent the action. A guard that must stop a write belongs on PreToolUse, before the call. The prompt is guidance, and exit code 2 after the fact cannot revert the file.
questions.constraint: the write must be blocked before it happens
breaks: timeout is irrelevant; the write has already happened by the time the hook fires
a prompt line is not an enforcement point
exit 2 on PostToolUse only shows stderr to Claude; it does not undo the write
questions.chapter: Hooks

questions.q: Engineers keep forgetting to run the formatter after Claude edits files, and the system prompt asking Claude to run it is followed only some of the time. Which approach makes formatting happen on every edit?
options: Repeat the formatting instruction at the start and end of every user message, so that the model sees it twice and follows it consistently
Add the formatter as an extra tool and set tool_choice to any on every request, so the model must call some tool before each response
Configure a PostToolUse hook on the edit tools that runs the formatter, so the action does not depend on the model choosing to run it
Ask the model to rate its own confidence that formatting was done and re-run the task when the rating falls below an agreed threshold
questions.explain: Hooks give deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them. A formatter that must follow every edit is the textbook PostToolUse hook; prompts and self-ratings leave the decision to the model.
questions.constraint: formatting must happen on every edit
breaks: repetition still leaves the action to the model's discretion
forcing some tool call does not guarantee the formatter is the tool or that it runs after each edit
a self-reported rating is not a deterministic check
questions.chapter: Hooks

questions.q: An Agent SDK app lets Claude call a process_refund tool. Policy says a person must confirm each refund before it runs, and the confirmation screen belongs to the application. Which mechanism fits?
options: Handle the call in the canUseTool callback, show the person the amount and order, and return allow or deny from their choice
List process_refund in allowed_tools so it is pre-approved, and ask Claude in the prompt to wait for a typed confirmation before it calls it
Set the permission mode to bypassPermissions during business hours, when staff are available, and rely on the audit log to catch mistakes later
Run process_refund in a subagent with its own context so its isolation prevents the main conversation from issuing the refund without review
questions.explain: The canUseTool callback exists for calls that still need approval after modes and rules have been applied, which is exactly where application-owned confirmation belongs. Pre-approval and bypass modes remove the checkpoint, and a subagent changes context, not authority.
questions.constraint: human confirmation owned by the application
breaks: pre-approval removes the checkpoint; a typed confirmation is only a request to the model
bypassPermissions skips approval entirely and the log only detects
subagent isolation separates context, not approval
questions.chapter: Production agents: workflow vs agent, wiring and human checkpoints

questions.q: A custom loop calls the Messages API with the web search server tool. Occasionally a task stops after the first response with stop_reason pause_turn, and the user sees an unfinished answer. The loop only continues when stop_reason is tool_use. Which change fixes the defect?
options: Treat pause_turn as an error and retry the original request unchanged, because the server tool simply failed and a fresh attempt should succeed
Raise max_tokens until pause_turn stops appearing, since the stop reason is produced when the answer is longer than the output budget allows
Treat pause_turn as not finished: send the assistant content back in a new request so the server-tool loop can continue until its work is done
Execute the pending tool call locally and append a tool_result block, because every non-end_turn stop reason means a client tool is waiting
questions.explain: pause_turn means a server-tool loop reached its iteration limit, and the documented action is to send the assistant content back to continue. Retrying unchanged repeats the work, and no client-side tool_result is owed for a server tool.
questions.constraint: loop only continues on tool_use
breaks: pause_turn means the server-tool loop paused at its iteration limit, not that it failed
that stop reason belongs to max_tokens, not pause_turn
a server tool runs on the platform; there is no client tool_result to supply
questions.chapter: Tool schemas, the tool-use loop and parallel calls

questions.q: An agent calls a flaky inventory tool. When the tool throws, the harness returns the raw stack trace as normal tool output. The agent then repeats the identical call 30 times before the run hits its cost cap. Which change corrects the pattern?
options: Return the failure as a tool_result with is_error set to true and a short actionable message, and cap how many retries the loop allows
Delete the tool_result entirely when a call fails, so the model has no failure text to react to and moves on to a different action by itself
Pass the full stack trace to the model with a note asking it to diagnose the server fault and fix it, because more detail always leads to better recovery
Raise the model's effort level so it reasons for longer before each call, since the repeated calls come from too little thinking on each turn
questions.explain: A failed client tool should be reported with is_error true so the model knows the call failed, and because the model might call the tool again the loop must cap retries. Missing results break the exchange, and a stack trace is not a recovery instruction.
questions.constraint: failed calls looping until a cost cap
breaks: every tool_use needs a matching tool_result; omitting it breaks the conversation
a stack trace is noise for the model and still carries no retry limit
effort does not give the harness a signal that the call failed or a way to stop
questions.chapter: Tool schemas, the tool-use loop and parallel calls

questions.q: A coaching assistant should remember each user's goals between conversations, but every new session starts blank. The team wants Claude to build up notes over time without keeping them all in the context window, and wants to control where the data lives. Which pattern fits?
options: A much larger context window for every request, so that the earlier conversations can be pasted in whole at the start of each new session
A server-side memory feature where the platform stores each user's notes on its own storage, which the team can neither inspect nor delete directly
A system prompt that tells Claude to remember what users say, which keeps the notes in the model's weights for use in later sessions with them
The memory tool: Claude requests file operations on a memory directory and the application runs them against storage the team controls
questions.explain: The memory tool lets Claude create, read, update and delete files that persist between sessions, and it operates client-side, so the application runs the operations and controls storage. A bigger window and a prompt instruction do not give durable, controllable memory.
questions.constraint: memory across sessions with team-controlled storage
breaks: pasting history grows cost and still hits limits; it is not durable memory
the memory tool is client-side, so the team owns storage and retention
nothing in a prompt changes weights or persists data
questions.chapter: Agent memory across sessions

questions.q: A support app built on the Agent SDK loses every conversation when the host process restarts. Users must be able to return to a specific earlier conversation, not only the latest. Which design meets this?
options: Keep the conversation in a process variable and rebuild it from the last user message after each restart, because the model can infer the rest
Store each conversation's session ID and pass it to resume when the user returns, so the SDK reloads that session's history
Use continue so the most recent session in the directory is resumed, since the user will always want the conversation that ended last
Fork the session on every restart to protect the original copy, then show the user whichever fork was created most recently on the host
questions.explain: Resuming a specific past session means capturing its session ID and passing it to resume; continue only picks up the most recent session. Fork is for exploring an alternative without losing the original.
questions.constraint: return to a chosen earlier conversation after a restart
breaks: the model cannot reconstruct earlier turns from the last message alone
continue picks the most recent session, not a chosen one
forking is for trying an alternative while keeping the original, not for locating a specific conversation
questions.chapter: Agent memory across sessions

questions.q: A coordinator agent delegates a code-review task to a subagent. The subagent keeps asking about decisions made earlier in the conversation because it starts with a fresh context. The coordinator's earlier discussion is essential to the review. Which fix is the most direct?
options: Raise the subagent's tool limit so it can call a search tool to retrieve earlier discussion, since a fresh context can always be rebuilt by search
Start the delegate as a fork, which copies the conversation so far instead of starting fresh, so the delegate sees the earlier discussion needed
Move every instruction into the subagent's description field so that the description acts as the shared conversation history for each new delegate
Merge the subagent back into the coordinator so one agent does everything, which removes context isolation along with the delegation overhead
questions.explain: A fork is a subagent that copies the conversation so far rather than starting fresh, which fits a task that depends on earlier discussion. Extra tools and a longer description do not transfer history, and merging gives up the benefit of delegation.
questions.constraint: the delegate needs the earlier conversation
breaks: tool access does not carry the conversation into the subagent
the description tells the parent when to use the subagent; it is not the conversation
this abandons delegation instead of passing the context it needs
questions.chapter: Using subagents effectively

questions.q: A streaming handler totals output tokens by adding the usage.output_tokens value from every message_delta event it receives. For a long answer the stream shows three such events, and the monthly report is roughly double what the billing page shows. What is wrong?
options: The usage field in message_delta counts only the tokens since the previous event, so the handler must add the values but also subtract the input tokens
Streaming responses are billed at twice the rate of non-streaming ones, so the report is correct and the billing page must be showing only half
The handler should sum the values from content_block_delta events instead, because message_delta events are only sent when a response is truncated
The usage counts in message_delta events are cumulative, so the handler should take the last value instead of adding them together
questions.explain: The token counts in a message_delta usage field are cumulative, so the final event already holds the total. Adding the events double-counts. Streaming has no price difference, and content_block_delta events carry content, not totals.
questions.constraint: three message_delta events, usage doubled
breaks: the values are running totals, not increments
streaming is not billed at a different token count
message_delta is sent for every message and content_block_delta events carry text, not usage totals
questions.chapter: Streamed responses and interrupted streams

questions.q: A tool-using app streams responses. When Claude calls a tool, the handler tries to run JSON.parse on the input_json_delta text of each delta as soon as it arrives, and throws on most of them. What is the correct approach?
options: Concatenate the partial_json strings for that content block and parse once, after the block's content_block_stop event, keyed by the block index
Ask the API to disable streaming for tool calls only, because partial tool input cannot be reassembled by a client once it has been split into deltas
Parse each delta separately and merge the resulting objects, since every delta is a complete JSON object describing one argument of the call
Wait for the message_stop event and parse the whole stream body as one JSON document, since the entire response is a single JSON value in the end
questions.explain: Tool input arrives as input_json_delta fragments carrying partial_json. The fragments are only valid JSON once joined, so the handler should accumulate them per content block (by index) and parse at content_block_stop. The stream as a whole is not one JSON document.
questions.constraint: partial JSON fragments in a streamed tool call
breaks: tool input can be reassembled; the deltas are designed to be concatenated
each delta is a fragment of a JSON string, not a complete object
the stream is a sequence of events, and only each block's input forms JSON
questions.chapter: Streamed responses and interrupted streams

questions.q: A service builds its tools array from a dictionary, so the order of the tool definitions changes between processes. Everything else in the request is identical, yet prompt-cache reads are near zero and cache writes happen on almost every request. Why?
options: Cache entries are keyed by request id, so no two requests can ever share an entry unless they are retried with exactly the same request id each time
Only the system prompt is eligible for caching, and tool definitions are always excluded, so a changing tools array just adds noise to the usage fields
Tools come first in the cached prefix, so a change in tool order changes the prefix and invalidates the cache from the start
The cache lifetime is shortened whenever more than one process writes to it, so concurrent services must raise the lifetime to the one-hour option instead
questions.explain: Prompt caching covers the prefix tools, then system, then messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Modifying tool definitions invalidates the whole cache, so a shuffled array has the same effect. Sorting the tools into a stable order restores reads.
questions.constraint: tool array order changes between processes
breaks: the cache matches on prefix content, not on a request id
tool definitions are part of the cached prefix
writers do not shorten the lifetime, and order changes would still break the match
questions.chapter: Rules of prompt caching

questions.q: A developer adds cache_control to a 900-token system prompt on a model whose minimum cacheable prompt is longer than that. The requests succeed with no error, but both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are 0. How should the developer read this?
options: The cache_control field was rejected silently because it can only be attached to tool definitions and never to the system prompt text block
The cache is warming up and reads will begin after the first five minutes, so the developer only needs to wait before expecting any cache activity
The API counted the tokens against the cache quota already, which is why both counters show zero until the daily quota resets for the organisation
The prompt is below the minimum cacheable length, so it was processed without caching and no error was raised, so nothing was written or read
questions.explain: Prompts shorter than the model's minimum are processed without caching and no error is returned; when both cache counters are 0 the prompt was not cached. The fix is to cache a longer stable prefix or accept that this prompt is too short to benefit.
questions.constraint: no error and zero cache counters
breaks: cache_control can be attached to system content; the cause is length
a cacheable prompt writes on the first request; zero writes means it was not cached
there is no daily cache quota that produces zero counters
questions.chapter: Rules of prompt caching

questions.q: A nightly job downloads the results of a Message Batches job to rebuild a report, but a re-run 40 days after submission finds that the results can no longer be downloaded. What explains this?
options: Batches expire if processing is not complete within 24 hours, so the job's results were discarded on the day after submission and none existed
Batch results are available for 29 days after creation; later you can still view the batch but not download its results
Results are deleted automatically once downloaded for the first time, so a second download is never possible even within the first day
Results stay available only while the custom_id values remain unique, and reusing one in a later batch removes the older result from the platform
questions.explain: Batch results remain available for 29 days after creation. After that the batch can still be viewed, but results cannot be downloaded. The 24-hour limit is the processing window, so it is a different clock.
questions.constraint: re-run 40 days after submission
breaks: the 24-hour limit is for processing; results remain for longer after completion
downloads do not consume the results within the retention period
custom_id uniqueness applies within a batch and does not delete other batches' results
questions.chapter: Images, PDFs, the Files API and Message Batches

questions.q: An agent loop answers a tool call by sending a user message whose content array holds a short text note first and the tool_result block second. The API rejects the request. What is the fix?
options: Send the text note in its own assistant message just before the tool result, because assistant turns may hold commentary about the pending call
Remove the tool_result and describe the output in the text note, since a plain text description of the tool output is accepted in its place
Put the tool_result blocks first in the content array and place any text after all of the tool results, as the API requires, results first
Set the note as a system message for that turn, because system content is the only place a note about a pending result can be sent
questions.explain: In the user message that returns tool results, the tool_result blocks must come first in the content array, with any text after them. Reordering the blocks fixes the request.
questions.constraint: tool_result must be first in the user turn
breaks: assistant turns do not carry the tool result and this breaks role order
the result must come back as a tool_result block matched to the tool_use
the system prompt is not changed per turn for this purpose; the order rule still applies
questions.chapter: Tool schemas, the tool-use loop and parallel calls

questions.q: A chat UI streams text into the page. Users sometimes see an answer that stops mid-sentence with no warning, and the logs show a stop reason of model_context_window_exceeded on those responses. What should the handler do?
options: Treat the response as truncated, flag it to the user, and shorten or restructure the input before trying again
Show the text as a complete answer, because that stop reason is sent when Claude has finished and the context window is simply full of the result
Resend the identical request with a higher max_tokens value, because this stop reason means the output limit was reached before the window was full
Resume the same stream automatically with a fresh connection, because the stop reason indicates a dropped connection that the client can recover
questions.explain: model_context_window_exceeded means the response filled the model's context window, and the documented handling is to treat the response as truncated. Distinguish it from max_tokens, which is the output cap you set, and from a dropped connection.
questions.constraint: stop reason is model_context_window_exceeded
breaks: the response was cut off because the window was filled, not finished
that stop reason is about the context window; max_tokens is a different limit
this is a stop reason on a finished message, not a transport failure
questions.chapter: Streamed responses and interrupted streams

questions.q: A document-analysis service receives the same 20 MB contract PDF with many different questions over a day, and each request re-uploads the file as base64. Requests are slow and sometimes rejected as too large. Which change addresses both problems?
options: Compress the base64 text with gzip before sending, since the API decompresses request bodies and the smaller payload avoids the limit
Split the PDF into single pages and send all pages with every question, so that each request stays below the size limit for each single page
Upload the file once through the Files API and reference its file_id in a document block for each question, rather than re-sending it
Reference the file as an image block with its file_id, because the image block type accepts any file type and skips the size checks
questions.explain: The Files API exists so content is uploaded once and referenced by file_id instead of re-sent with each request. PDFs are referenced in document blocks; images use image blocks.
questions.constraint: same large PDF re-sent many times
breaks: the API expects the documented content blocks, not a compressed body
this still re-sends everything for every question and multiplies the content
image blocks are for image files; a PDF is referenced in a document block
questions.chapter: Code execution and the Files API

questions.q: A team's Agent SDK worker runs in a container built from the repository, which contains a CLAUDE.md with instructions meant only for human developers using Claude Code. In production the worker follows those instructions unexpectedly. The team wants the agent to use only what the application passes in code. What should they do?
options: Pass an empty settingSources list so the SDK loads no filesystem settings, and supply the system prompt and options in code
Delete the CLAUDE.md from the repository, since the SDK has no other way of being told to ignore a project instruction file that exists on disk
Rename the file to claude.md in lower case, because the SDK only loads project instructions when the file name uses the exact upper-case spelling
Set the permission mode to plan for the worker, because plan mode makes the agent ignore any project instructions while it prepares its work
questions.explain: When settingSources is omitted, query() reads the same filesystem settings as the CLI, including CLAUDE.md files and .claude/ skills and agents. Passing an empty list limits the agent to what the application configures programmatically.
questions.constraint: SDK worker picking up developer instructions
breaks: the SDK can be told to ignore filesystem settings without removing files developers use
renaming does not control which settings sources the SDK loads
permission modes do not control which instruction files are loaded
questions.chapter: Durable project context: CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks and subagents

questions.q: A chat feature built directly on the Messages API loses track of earlier turns: each user message is answered as if it were the first. The code sends only the latest user message in the messages array. What is the correct design?
options: Send a stable session identifier with each request so the API retrieves the stored turns on its side and appends them automatically
Enable prompt caching on the latest message, which makes the platform remember the earlier turns of the conversation for later calls
Ask Claude in the system prompt to remember the previous questions, which makes the model keep them from one request to the next
Keep the conversation history in the application and send the previous user and assistant turns with each new request, every time
questions.explain: Each turn's earlier messages occupy the context window and are preserved only because they are sent again, so the application must resend the history. Caching can make the repeated prefix cheaper, but only if it is sent.
questions.constraint: each request answered as the first one
breaks: the Messages API does not store the conversation between requests
caching reduces the cost of a repeated prefix; it does not supply history you did not send
the model keeps nothing between independent requests
questions.chapter: Context engineering: window, compaction, clearing and subagent handoffs

questions.q: An internal tool lets customers paste free text that is placed inside the system prompt, ahead of the instructions that define the assistant's role. A tester pastes a line telling the assistant to ignore its role, and it complies. Which change to what crosses the application boundary best addresses this?
options: Move the customer text to the very end of the system prompt, so that the role instructions above it carry more weight than the pasted line
Keep the role and rules in the system prompt, and pass the customer's text in a user turn clearly delimited as data to be processed
Strip every sentence that contains the word ignore from the customer's text before inserting it, so that the known attack phrase cannot appear
Tell customers in the interface that pasting instructions is not allowed, and treat any breach as a policy violation reported afterwards
questions.explain: Untrusted content should not sit in the privileged system prompt. Keeping rules in the system prompt and passing customer text as delimited data in a user turn changes what crosses the boundary. Keyword stripping and warnings are weaker than structure.
questions.constraint: customer text inserted into the system prompt
breaks: untrusted text is still in the privileged system prompt
a keyword filter misses paraphrases and blocks legitimate text
a notice is not a control; the text still reaches the system prompt
questions.chapter: Security: injection, untrusted input, scoped identity and secrets

questions.q: A production service calls Claude with a model identifier copied from a tutorial. The team wants upgrades to happen only after regression evaluations pass, never silently. Which configuration practice supports this?
options: Use the shortest alias available for the model so the service always receives the newest snapshot without any configuration change being needed
Use the full pinned model ID in configuration and change it in a reviewed release after the regression evaluations pass, and never silently
Read the model name from the user's browser settings at request time, so each customer's session picks the model that suits their device best
Leave the model unset so that the platform picks the current default for each request, which keeps the service on the best model available
questions.explain: Each Claude model ID identifies a pinned version of the model, so putting the full ID in configuration and promoting a new one through a reviewed change makes upgrades deliberate. Floating aliases or defaults can change behaviour without the regression gate.
questions.constraint: upgrades must follow regression evaluations
breaks: an alias that moves lets the model change without a reviewed release
model choice should not vary by untrusted client input or bypass evaluation
an unset or floating choice changes behaviour without a regression gate
questions.chapter: Platform choice and versioning what ships

questions.q: A developer's .claude/settings.local.json allows a command that the organisation's managed settings deny. On the developer's machine Claude Code still refuses the command. Which statement about configuration explains this?
options: Project settings always win over everything else, and the refusal comes from the project's shared file that happens to contain an older rule
The local file is read only when the project is first opened, so the developer must restart the machine for the change to take effect
Command-line flags override managed settings, so the developer should pass the allow rule on the command line every time the tool is started
Managed settings sit at the highest level of precedence, so a lower level cannot override them for the same key
questions.explain: Settings precedence runs managed, command line, project local, shared project, then user. A key set at a higher level overrides the same key lower down, so a local allow cannot override a managed deny.
questions.constraint: local allow versus managed deny
breaks: project settings rank below managed settings
precedence, not a restart, decides the outcome
the command line ranks below managed settings
questions.chapter: Durable project context: CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks and subagents

questions.q: A team ships a Claude Code plugin that depends on another team's plugin for its MCP server. After the other team publishes a breaking release, the first plugin stops working for everyone who updates. Which change prevents a repeat?
options: Declare a version constraint on the dependency, a semantic-version range the team has tested against, in the plugin's manifest
Copy the other plugin's files into the first plugin's folder so that nothing outside the repository can change what the plugin loads
Ask every user to disable automatic updates on their machines, so that no plugin is ever upgraded without a manual review by that user
Remove the dependency declaration entirely, since an undeclared plugin is installed at the version the user already has on the machine
questions.explain: A dependency tracks the latest version its marketplace provides unless a version constraint is declared. A semantic-version range such as ^2.0 limits it to versions the team has tested.
questions.constraint: breaking release in a plugin dependency
breaks: copying forks the code and loses fixes the dependency's maintainers ship
pushes the burden to each user and does not pin the tested range
without a declaration the dependency is not installed or constrained for the user
questions.chapter: Skills, custom commands and plugins

questions.q: A client library sees HTTP 429 responses carrying a retry-after header and retries after a fixed 100 ms. The retries keep failing and make the congestion worse. Which behaviour matches the API's documented semantics?
options: Retry immediately and as often as possible, because a 429 means the request was not counted and a faster retry gets a slot sooner
Treat the 429 as a permanent failure and surface it to the user without any retry, because rate limits never clear within a session
Wait for the number of seconds in the retry-after header before retrying, and limit the number of attempts
Switch to a larger model on every 429, since only the smaller model's limits are low and a larger one would accept the request at once
questions.explain: When the response has a retry-after header, the client should wait that long before retrying, and retries should be limited. The SDKs already follow retry-after and x-should-retry; hand-written clients should do the same.
questions.constraint: 429 with retry-after header
breaks: hammering a rate-limited endpoint prolongs the problem
rate limits are replenished continuously, so waiting works
model switching is not the documented response to a rate limit
questions.chapter: Resilience: retriable vs terminal errors

questions.q: An integration retries every 429 up to ten times with backoff. One afternoon the retries all fail for hours; the responses have no retry-after header, and the dashboard shows the organisation has reached its monthly spend cap. What is the right handling?
options: Increase the retry count to fifty with a longer backoff, because the cap is replenished continuously like a per-minute request limit
Switch the traffic to the batch endpoint for the rest of the month, because batch requests are not counted against the organisation's spend limits
Add the retry-after header yourself to the next request, since the server uses the client's header to decide when the cap is lifted
Stop retrying, alert the owner and fail fast, because a spend-cap 429 keeps failing until access resumes, so retrying only adds load
questions.explain: A tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and keeps failing until access resumes, so retrying wastes effort. The code should limit retries after a 429 and raise an alert so the cap can be addressed.
questions.constraint: 429 with no retry-after during a spend cap
breaks: a spend cap does not replenish like a rate limit
batch usage is still billed and the cap still applies
retry-after is a response header; the client cannot set it to lift a cap
questions.chapter: Resilience: retriable vs terminal errors

questions.q: A streaming endpoint returns HTTP 200 and begins sending events. Halfway through, an event of type error with overloaded_error arrives and the stream ends. The client code only checks the HTTP status before streaming and shows a half-finished answer as complete. What should change?
options: Check the status code again after the stream closes, because the 200 is replaced by a 529 once the server notices the overload has occurred
Handle error events inside the stream: stop, mark the answer incomplete and retry or fail, rather than relying on the HTTP status
Ignore the event, because overloaded errors inside a stream are informational and the partial text already received is complete enough to show
Disable streaming for all requests, since errors can only be detected reliably when the entire response arrives in a single non-streaming payload
questions.explain: Errors can be sent in the event stream, and an overloaded_error there normally corresponds to an HTTP 529 in a non-streaming context. Because the 200 has already been sent, the client must read the error event and treat the response as unfinished.
questions.constraint: error event after an HTTP 200
breaks: the HTTP status was already sent as 200; it is not rewritten
the event means the response did not finish
streaming is recommended for long requests and the stream's errors can be handled
questions.chapter: Streamed responses and interrupted streams

questions.q: A new deployment's calls to Claude fail with 401 in one environment and 403 in another. In the first, the key was revoked last week. In the second, a valid key calls a model the workspace has not been granted. Which diagnosis matches the API's error semantics?
options: Both codes mean the key is invalid, and 403 is only returned when the invalid key was sent over a connection that is not encrypted
401 means the request body is malformed and 403 means the request was too large, so both are fixed by editing the payload sent by the client
401 is an authentication problem with the key, such as revoked or expired; 403 means the key is valid but lacks permission for the resource
401 means the service is overloaded and 403 means the rate limit was hit, so both are fixed by retrying later with exponential backoff
questions.explain: 401 authentication_error means a problem with the API key such as malformed, revoked or expired. 403 permission_error means the key does not have permission to use the specified resource. Neither is fixed by retrying.
questions.constraint: 401 versus 403
breaks: 403 is about permission, not transport security
malformed and oversized requests return 400 and 413
overload is 529 and rate limits are 429, neither of which is 401 or 403
questions.chapter: Resilience: retriable vs terminal errors

questions.q: A report generator sends a very long non-streaming request and intermittently receives a timeout error after a long wait. Which change follows the API guidance for long-running requests?
options: Use the streaming Messages API for the long request, so output begins arriving and the connection is not idle for the whole generation
Retry the same non-streaming request three times in parallel and use whichever response comes back first, to hedge against the timeout
Lower max_tokens to a very small value so each response is short, and ask the model to continue in separate follow-up requests afterwards
Remove the system prompt from the request, because system text makes a long request time out in a way that user text does not
questions.explain: For long-running Messages API requests the API guidance is to use the streaming Messages API. Retrying in parallel and cutting output do not address the cause.
questions.constraint: intermittent timeouts on long requests
breaks: multiplies cost and does not change the long-wait pattern
may truncate useful output and does not address the request design
the system prompt is not the cause of long-running timeouts
questions.chapter: Streamed responses and interrupted streams

questions.q: An ingestion service handles uploads of PDFs, plain text files and screenshots through the Files API. It sends every uploaded file_id inside an image content block, and PDF uploads fail while screenshots work. What is the defect?
options: The Files API only supports images, so PDFs and plain text files must be converted to screenshots before they are uploaded and referenced
The file_id values for PDFs expire after one minute, so the service must upload each PDF again immediately before every request that uses it
The content block type must match the file type: PDFs and plain text go in document blocks and images go in image blocks, per the file type
Image blocks accept any file type when the MIME type is set to application/pdf in the request, so the upload call must set that value correctly
questions.explain: The documented mapping is PDF and plain text to document blocks, images (jpeg, png, gif, webp) to image blocks, and other datasets to container_upload. A PDF sent in an image block is the defect.
questions.constraint: multi-format ingestion through the Files API
breaks: PDFs and text are supported and referenced in document blocks
nothing in the mapping points to a one-minute expiry; the block type is wrong
the block type is determined by the file type, not by overriding the MIME type
questions.chapter: Code execution and the Files API

questions.q: A monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md and a packages/billing/CLAUDE.md with rules for the billing code. A developer works only in packages/web and asks why the billing rules never appear in that session. Which statement is correct?
options: Nested CLAUDE.md files load on demand, once Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory, so billing rules stay out of a web-only session
Only the root CLAUDE.md is ever read, so any CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory is ignored by Claude Code and should be moved up into the root file
Nested files load at launch for every package but are given a lower rank, so the billing rules are present and simply outweighed by web rules
The billing file loads only when the developer types its path as an import line into the prompt, since subdirectory files are never read automatically
questions.explain: CLAUDE.md files above the working directory load at launch, while files in subdirectories load once Claude reads, writes or edits another file there. This keeps unrelated rules out of context, and it explains why a nested rule can appear to be missing early in a session.
questions.constraint: billing rules absent from a web-only session
breaks: subdirectory files are loaded, just on demand
they are not loaded at launch, so there is nothing to outweigh
no manual import is needed; reading a file in that directory loads it
questions.chapter: Durable project context: CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks and subagents

questions.q: Midway through a long session a developer told Claude in chat to always use the repository's logging helper. After /compact, Claude stops following that instruction. What is the most durable fix?
options: Repeat the instruction in chat after every compaction, since compaction deletes all earlier instructions and nothing on disk can survive it
Disable compaction for the session, because a summary of the conversation always drops any instruction that was written in chat form
Ask Claude to treat the instruction as higher priority than the others, because priority wording is kept verbatim through every compaction
Put the instruction in the project's root CLAUDE.md, which Claude re-reads from disk and re-injects after compaction, on every compaction
questions.explain: Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction because Claude re-reads it from disk. An instruction given only in conversation is the usual reason one disappears after compaction. Writing rules where they persist is the durable fix.
questions.constraint: instruction given only in conversation
breaks: files on disk survive compaction, so repeating in chat is unnecessary
disabling compaction forgoes a feature instead of recording the rule where it persists
wording priority does not make a chat-only instruction survive compaction
questions.chapter: Steering Long Sessions

questions.q: A team needs three Claude Code workers on one refactor, where the frontend worker must negotiate an interface directly with the backend worker while a third reviews both. Plain subagents that only report back to the lead have not worked. Which Claude Code feature fits, and what is its main cost?
options: A single subagent with three tools, because one subagent can hold all three roles and talks to itself, which is cheaper than coordinating workers
Agent teams: teammates work in their own context windows and message each other directly, at the cost of extra coordination overhead and more tokens
Three headless runs started in parallel from a shell script, because separate processes automatically share one conversation and exchange messages with one another through the shared repository
Agent teams with the same cost as one session, because teammates share a single context window and only the lead pays for the tokens used
questions.explain: Teammates work independently, each in its own context window, and communicate directly with each other. That fits negotiation between workers, but it adds coordination overhead and uses significantly more tokens than a single session. For sequential or same-file work, one session or subagents are more effective.
questions.constraint: workers must talk to each other
breaks: one subagent cannot negotiate between independent workers' contexts
separate runs share nothing unless something connects them
teammates each have their own context window, which is why more tokens are used
questions.chapter: Durable project context: CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks and subagents

questions.q: Claude Code creates a git worktree for a parallel task, but tests in it fail because the .env file and installed dependencies are missing, although both exist in the main checkout. What should the team do?
options: Commit the .env file to the repository so every checkout, including worktrees, receives it through version control, along with the dependencies
List the gitignored files to copy in a .worktreeinclude file at the repo root, and run dependency installation as part of worktree setup
Symlink the worktree's folder to the main checkout so both directories point to the same files, even while the two tasks edit them in parallel
Run the tests only in the main checkout and treat the worktree failures as expected, since a worktree is not meant to run the test suite at all
questions.explain: A worktree is a fresh checkout, so gitignored files such as .env and installed dependencies are not there. A .worktreeinclude file at the repo root lists the gitignored files Claude Code should copy into every worktree it creates; dependencies still need installing.
questions.constraint: worktree missing .env and dependencies
breaks: committing secrets to git creates a security problem
a shared directory defeats the isolation that worktrees provide
tests need to run in the worktree for parallel work to be useful
questions.chapter: Explore-plan-code loop and permission modes

questions.q: A team has a /deploy workflow with real side effects. They want it to run only when a developer types the command, never because Claude decided that the conversation seemed to call for it. Which setting achieves this?
options: Write a precise description of when to deploy, because a careful description makes Claude invoke the skill only in the situations intended
Restrict the skill's allowed tools to read-only tools, which makes Claude unable to invoke a skill whose tools could change anything
Place the skill in the user's home directory rather than the repository, since skills outside the project are never offered to Claude
Add disable-model-invocation: true to the skill or command's frontmatter, so only the user can invoke it
questions.explain: Adding disable-model-invocation: true to the frontmatter stops Claude from invoking it on its own, leaving invocation to the person typing the command. A description or tool list shapes behaviour but does not remove the model's ability to invoke it.
questions.constraint: side-effecting workflow only on explicit command
breaks: a description guides, but it does not forbid automatic invocation
tool limits do not control who may invoke the skill
personal skills are available to Claude too; location does not stop invocation
questions.chapter: Skills vs. other Claude Code features

questions.q: A platform team wants to give all fifteen repositories the same bundle: three skills, a formatting hook and an MCP server configuration, installed and updated together. Which mechanism fits?
options: A plugin, because it packages skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit, usually from a marketplace
A shared CLAUDE.md file copied into each repository, because a single instruction file can carry skills, hooks and server configuration together
A standalone skill with a long description, because one skill folder is the unit that bundles hooks and MCP servers for an organisation
A subagent definition that lists every item as a tool, since a subagent file is how a set of hooks and servers is distributed to repositories
questions.explain: A plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers or other components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit, which is the packaging format for a bundle used across repositories.
questions.constraint: distribute a mixed bundle to many repos
breaks: CLAUDE.md holds instructions; it does not package hooks or server configs
a skill packages one capability, not a mixed bundle
a subagent is a delegate with its own context, not a distribution format
questions.chapter: Skills, custom commands and plugins

questions.q: A repository defines 25 subagents, each with a long, detailed description, and Claude Code shows a warning at startup about the combined descriptions exceeding a token budget. Sessions also feel slower to start. Which fix addresses the cause?
options: Delete half of the subagents at random so the combined descriptions fall below the limit, since the number of subagents is all that matters
Rename the subagent files with shorter names, because the warning is triggered by file name length and not by the description text inside
Trim each description to when to use the subagent and move the detail into its system prompt, which loads only when it runs
Move all subagent descriptions into the root CLAUDE.md so they load once, which keeps them out of the part of context the warning measures
questions.explain: Subagent descriptions sit in context so Claude can choose a delegate, which is why they should be short. When combined descriptions exceed 15,000 tokens a warning appears, and the recommended fix is to trim descriptions and move detail into each subagent's system prompt.
questions.constraint: descriptions exceed the token budget
breaks: removal at random drops useful agents instead of fixing the oversized descriptions
the warning counts description tokens, not file names
this moves the same text into always-loaded context
questions.chapter: Using subagents effectively

questions.q: A team upgrades Claude Code and worries that its older .claude/commands/ markdown files for slash commands will stop working now that skills exist. What is the accurate position?
options: They stop working and must be rewritten as plugins first, because commands are not recognised once the skills feature is enabled by default
They work, but only when each file is also registered in a settings file that lists every command by name for the project
They work only for the user who created them, because command files are always personal and cannot be shared through a repository
Existing command files keep working, and a command can be moved into a skill folder later, where the folder name becomes the command
questions.explain: Custom commands have been merged into skills, and existing .claude/commands/ files keep working. Moving one to .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md keeps the same /name command.
questions.constraint: worry about legacy command files
breaks: existing command files continue to work
no registration step is required
project command files are shared with the repository
questions.chapter: Skills, custom commands and plugins

questions.q: A team is building a golden set to evaluate a ticket-summarisation prompt. Which composition is the most useful starting point?
options: A few hundred tickets that Claude itself wrote to look typical, since synthetic examples are cheaper to produce and keep the set perfectly balanced
Real, anonymised tickets sampled from production, plus deliberately hard edge cases, each with an expected outcome agreed by reviewers
The five tickets the team remembers best, because well-known cases are the ones stakeholders will check first when a new version is released
Only tickets that the current prompt already handles well, so that the evaluation shows a stable baseline whenever the prompt is edited later
questions.explain: A golden set should resemble production and include the cases that go wrong, with an expected result agreed in advance. Synthetic-only, tiny or success-only sets give a comfortable number that says little about real behaviour.
questions.constraint: building a first golden set
breaks: synthetic tickets can miss the real distribution and its messy cases
a handful of memorable cases is too small and biased
excluding failures hides the very cases a change should improve
questions.chapter: Eval suites, grading methods and calibrating an LLM judge

questions.q: A team uses Claude as a judge to score summaries from 1 to 5. Before using the scores to decide whether a prompt change ships, what should they do?
options: Trust the judge because it is a strong model, and only revisit the scores if a customer complains about summary quality after the release
Ask the same judge to grade its own scoring on a second pass, and ship the change if the two passes give identical numbers for the sample
Have people label a sample, compare the judge's scores with the human labels, and refine the rubric until agreement is acceptable
Average the scores over many runs so the noise cancels out, and treat the average as the true quality of the summaries for the decision
questions.explain: An LLM-as-judge is an instrument that needs calibrating: compare it with human-labelled data and fix the rubric until agreement is acceptable. A consistent judge can still be consistently wrong.
questions.constraint: using a model judge to gate a prompt change
breaks: model strength does not establish agreement with human judgement
self-agreement measures consistency, not validity
averaging reduces noise but not a systematic mismatch with human judgement
questions.chapter: Eval suites, grading methods and calibrating an LLM judge

questions.q: A classification prompt scores 92% on the golden set in one run and 88% in the next with the same model and no changes. The team wonders whether the prompt is unstable. Which interpretation and action fit?
options: Sampling makes outputs non-deterministic, so run each case several times and compare pass rates, not single runs, before and after a change
The run-to-run gap proves a bug in the evaluation harness, so the harness should be rewritten before any more results are taken seriously by the rest of the team
Four points is within the margin that every evaluation shows, so a single run is always enough and no repeated runs are ever needed
The prompt must be unstable only if the gap exceeds ten points, so smaller gaps can be ignored without checking how they were produced
questions.explain: Generation is non-deterministic, so one run is a noisy estimate. Running each case several times and comparing pass rates gives a fairer before-and-after comparison.
questions.constraint: same prompt, different scores between runs
breaks: variation can come from sampling itself rather than from a bug
single runs can mislead when the difference of interest is small
there is no fixed ten-point threshold; the variance should be measured
questions.chapter: Tokens, the context window and non-determinism

questions.q: A feature extracts invoice fields into JSON, and a reviewer proposes scoring every output with a model judge asking whether it "looks right". Which evaluation design is better?
options: Use the judge for everything, since a single scoring method is easier to explain and the judge can also compare numbers against the labels
Compare outputs to the labels by exact string match only, including whitespace and key order, so that anything slightly different counts as a failure
Check structure and field values with deterministic assertions against the labelled answers, and reserve a judge for qualities code cannot check
Skip evaluation until the feature is live and use customer complaints as the signal, since complaints measure the quality that really matters
questions.explain: Where an answer is checkable, deterministic assertions on parsed fields are exact, cheap and repeatable. A judge belongs where a person would need to read for qualities such as tone or completeness.
questions.constraint: extraction with known correct values
breaks: deterministic checks are cheaper, exact and repeatable for fields with known answers
overly strict matching fails correct outputs that differ only in formatting
complaints arrive late and cover only a fraction of errors
questions.chapter: Eval suites, grading methods and calibrating an LLM judge

questions.q: A team plans to move from one Claude model to a newer one. The new model is cheaper and scores higher overall on the team's golden set, but a slice of 40 refund-policy cases drops from 95% to 80%. What should the release decision be?
options: Investigate and fix the refund-policy regression, or hold the migration for that slice, because an overall gain can hide a drop that matters
Ship the new model, since the overall score improved and a regression in one slice is expected whenever a model is replaced by a newer one
Discard the golden set and write a new one that the new model passes, since a set it fails on is evidently out of date for the new model
Ship to all users and raise the temperature for refund questions, because added randomness will let the new model recover the lost accuracy on that slice of cases
questions.explain: Regression evaluations exist to catch behaviour changes across releases. An overall improvement can mask a slice that matters, so the slice should be investigated, the prompt adapted and re-tested, or the migration held.
questions.constraint: overall score up, one slice down 15 points
breaks: an aggregate gain does not make a 15-point slice drop acceptable
rewriting the test to pass defeats its purpose
temperature does not repair a systematic policy regression
questions.chapter: Eval suites, grading methods and calibrating an LLM judge

questions.q: A support assistant answers questions about a product catalogue. It confidently quotes a warranty period that does not appear in any document it was given. Traces show the retrieved passages contain no warranty information. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Lower the temperature to zero so that the model stops inventing details and always repeats the exact figures it saw during its training
Add more catalogue documents to the prompt on every request, since a larger context makes any missing detail appear somewhere in it
Switch to a larger model, because larger models never state a figure that is absent from the documents they have been supplied with
Instruct the assistant to answer only from the supplied documents and to say the information was not found when it is absent from them
questions.explain: The documents lack the answer and the prompt gives the model no way to decline, so it produces a plausible one. Grounding the answer in the supplied documents and returning "not found" when they do not contain it addresses the cause.
questions.constraint: hallucinated figure absent from the sources
breaks: temperature does not give the model the missing facts or permission to say not found
more text does not help when the source has no warranty information
model size does not guarantee grounding without instructions to stay within the documents
questions.chapter: Test and tracing layers

questions.q: A request that worked yesterday now comes back with stop_reason refusal. The prompt is unchanged. What is the right handling in the integration code?
options: Retry the identical request up to five times with backoff, because a refusal is a transient server error that resolves by waiting a few seconds
Read the stop details, route the case to a safe path, and use a fallback model where policy allows, instead of retrying the same request
Treat the empty or partial text as the answer and show it, since the response finished normally and a refusal is just a short assistant reply
Add the word please to the prompt and send it again, because a refusal is only a tone problem that a politer instruction resolves each time
questions.explain: For a refusal stop reason the documented action is to read stop_details and retry on a fallback model. Retrying the identical request repeats the refusal at extra cost, and the text is not a normal answer.
questions.constraint: stop reason refusal on an unchanged prompt
breaks: a refusal is a model decision, not a transient failure
the stop reason says Claude declined, so it should not be shown as a normal answer
wording tweaks are not a documented handling and may repeat the refusal
questions.chapter: Resilience: retriable vs terminal errors

questions.q: Users report that an assistant ignores its formatting rules. Prompt engineers rewrite the prompt three times without success. A developer then logs the raw request body and finds that the system field arrives empty because of a templating bug. What does this show?
options: The model is ignoring instructions, so the prompt should be made longer and louder until the formatting rules are followed in every reply
The failure was in the integration layer, not model output, so inspecting what was actually sent should come before rewriting prompts
The templating bug is a model failure, because the model should have refused to answer when its system prompt was missing from the request
Nothing can be concluded without a larger evaluation set, because one request body is too small a sample to show anything about the system
questions.explain: Isolating the origin means checking whether the integration layer sent what was intended before blaming the model. Logging the raw request exposed the empty system field. Every response also carries a request-id header, which helps correlate such a log with the API's record.
questions.constraint: prompt rewrites do not fix the formatting
breaks: the model never received the instructions
a missing prompt is a request-construction defect, not a model behaviour
a single logged request showing an empty field is conclusive evidence for that defect
questions.chapter: Test and tracing layers

questions.q: A long-running assistant follows a customer's constraint ("never suggest vendor X") for the first dozen turns, then starts recommending vendor X after about sixty turns. Traces show the constraint exists only in turn 3. Which diagnosis and fix fit?
options: Hallucination, so the fix is to ask the model to double-check every recommendation against its own earlier answers before replying each time it produces a recommendation for the customer
Under-acting, so the fix is to force a tool call on every turn with tool_choice set to any, which makes the model check the constraint first
Format drift, so the fix is a JSON schema on the reply, since a schema will keep an earlier user constraint in force on every later turn
Context loss: the constraint lives only in the history, so move it into the system prompt or persistent instructions and keep it out of trimmed content
questions.explain: A constraint stated once in conversation can be dropped when the history is summarised, trimmed or diluted. Putting durable rules in the system prompt (or other persistent instructions) keeps them in force for the whole session.

questions.q: A support chatbot's system prompt and tool definitions are cached, but each conversation adds many turns and most input tokens now sit in the growing message history, which is billed in full every turn. Which change cuts cost the most?
